questions.stem: What does the novella's first sentence reveal?
options: That Santiago Nasar is going to be killed that day
That the narrator has returned to the town to marry
That Angela Vicario has been returned by her husband
That the bishop is coming to bless Angela's wedding
questions.explanation: The opening tells us that 'they were going to kill' Santiago Nasar on the day it describes. The ending is given away at once, so the question becomes how and why it happened.

questions.stem: Why is Santiago Nasar up early on the morning he dies?
options: To wait at the dock for the bishop's boat
To ride out to inspect his father's ranch
To leave town before the Vicario twins find him
To help clear up after the wedding celebrations
questions.explanation: The whole town is excited about the bishop's visit. The bishop's boat passes without stopping, and he blesses the crowd from the deck, a sign of how little the church helps the town.

questions.stem: Why does Bayardo San Román return Angela Vicario to her family on their wedding night?
options: He finds she has been writing letters to Santiago
He hears that her brothers have threatened his life
He discovers that she is not a virgin
He learns that her family is poorer than they claimed
questions.explanation: In the town's code of honour, a bride must be a virgin. Bayardo brings her back to her mother's house within hours, and the family's disgrace sets off everything that follows.

questions.stem: What happens when Angela's family demands to know who was responsible?
options: After her brothers threaten her, she refuses to name anyone
After the priest questions her, she names the narrator's brother
After being beaten by her mother, she names Santiago Nasar
After a night of silence, she names Cristo Bedoya
questions.explanation: Angela is beaten by her mother and questioned by her brothers, and she names Santiago. The novella never confirms that he was responsible, and the narrator finds no evidence that he was.

questions.stem: What do the Vicario twins do after Angela names Santiago?
options: They challenge him to a public duel in the square after Mass
They tell almost everyone they meet that they are going to kill him
They wait in secret at his house so that no one will see them coming
They ask the mayor to arrest him for dishonouring their family
questions.explanation: The twins announce their plan at the meat market, at Clotilde Armenta's shop and elsewhere. Their openness suggests that, in part, they hope someone will stop them.

questions.stem: What does Colonel Lázaro Aponte, the mayor, do when he hears of the twins' plan?
options: He locks the twins in the town jail until the bishop's boat has safely left
He warns Santiago himself, but Santiago refuses to believe him
He orders the police to guard Santiago's house for the whole day
He takes away their knives and sends them home, thinking the danger is over
questions.explanation: Aponte confiscates the knives and treats the twins as bluffers. They simply fetch new knives. His half-hearted action is one of many failures by people who could have prevented the murder.

questions.stem: Why doesn't Santiago get the warning note that someone pushes under his door?
options: Victoria Guzmán hides it because she wants him to die
The twins take it back before anyone in the house wakes
It lies unseen on the floor, so no one reads it in time
His mother finds it first and burns it without reading it
questions.explanation: A note warning him is slipped under the door but no one sees it in time. It is one of many coincidences that, together with the town's silence, let the death happen.

questions.stem: Why can't Santiago get into his house when the twins chase him?
options: The servants have locked the door on the orders of the mayor
He has lost his key at the dock while watching the bishop's boat
His mother has barred the front door, believing he is already inside
The twins have locked the front door and are waiting for him in the street
questions.explanation: Plácida Linero, thinking her son is safe upstairs, bolts the door to keep the twins out. He is killed against the door she closed to protect him, a cruel irony.

questions.stem: Where does Santiago finally die?
options: In the town square, in front of the whole crowd that gathered
In the kitchen of his own house, after walking around to the back
On the dock, where he had gone to watch the bishop's boat
In Clotilde Armenta's milk shop, where the twins were waiting
questions.explanation: Stabbed many times at the front door, he walks more than a hundred yards around to the back of the house and falls in the kitchen.

questions.stem: What happens to the Vicario twins after the murder?
options: They spend three years in jail awaiting trial, then are acquitted
They are tried within a week, found guilty and sentenced to death
They escape into the mountains and are never brought to trial at all
They are convicted, but pardoned after a short time in prison
questions.explanation: The twins claim they killed to defend their family's honour. They are acquitted, which shows how far the community and the law accept that code.

questions.stem: What happens between Angela and Bayardo in the years after the murder?
options: She writes to him every week for seventeen years, and he finally returns
She marries Santiago's friend Cristo Bedoya and never speaks of Bayardo
He sends her a letter every week, but she burns them all unopened
He returns the next year to beg her forgiveness, and she refuses to see him
questions.explanation: Angela comes to love Bayardo only after he rejects her. He returns carrying nearly two thousand letters, none of them opened. The reunion turns part of a story of a crime into a strange love story.

questions.stem: How is the novella structured?
options: It follows each twin in turn through the day, and ends with their trial and sentence in court
It tells the events in strict chronological order, ending with the twins' acquittal
It describes the murder in full first, then traces the town's grief in later years
It keeps circling back to the same morning from new angles, and tells the murder itself last
questions.explanation: The narrative keeps returning to the same few hours, adding witnesses and details. The killing is only described fully in the last chapter, so the suspense is about how it could happen, not whether.

questions.stem: Who narrates the novella?
options: An unnamed friend of Santiago who returns to the town years later to investigate
Angela Vicario, looking back on her wedding night from old age in another town
An omniscient third-person narrator who knows every character's private thoughts
Santiago's friend Cristo Bedoya, recalling the morning years later
questions.explanation: The narrator was in the town that day and grew up with Santiago. Twenty-seven years later he gathers witnesses' memories and old records, like a journalist.

questions.stem: Which description best fits Santiago Nasar?
options: A wealthy, cheerful young man of Arab descent, twenty-one years old
A poor farm worker who has recently arrived in the town from the coast
A middle-aged ranch owner who has long been feared by the whole town
A shy student home from university who rarely leaves his mother's house
questions.explanation: Santiago inherited his father's ranch and is popular, handsome and rich. His wealth and status may help explain why some townspeople did not mind the danger he was in.

questions.stem: Bayardo San Román is best described as:
options: a priest who comes to the town with the bishop and stays to marry Angela
a modest young man whom Angela chose herself, against her family's wishes
a rich, mysterious outsider who wins Angela's family over with his wealth
a poor local fisherman who has loved Angela since they were children
questions.explanation: Bayardo arrives from elsewhere, spends lavishly and buys a fine house from the widower Xius. Angela is pushed to marry him because her family sees him as a prize.

questions.stem: How are the Vicario twins, Pedro and Pablo, presented?
options: As religious fanatics driven by faith rather than by family honour
As hot-tempered youths who kill Santiago in a sudden drunken fight
As reluctant killers who seem to want to be stopped, yet carry out the deed
As cold, eager murderers who keep their plan hidden from the rest of the town
questions.explanation: The twins are pig butchers who announce their plan to everyone, and one of them hesitates along the way. They feel bound by honour to act, which makes them both perpetrators and prisoners of the code.

questions.stem: Why is Victoria Guzmán's silence on the morning of the murder significant?
options: She does not know about the threat, which shows how few people in town had heard
She warns Santiago twice, but he laughs at her and goes out anyway
She tries to stop the twins herself, but they push her out of the way
She knows the twins are waiting but does not warn him, hinting at buried resentment
questions.explanation: The cook has heard of the plan and says nothing. Her daughter later suggests she secretly wanted Santiago dead, linked to how the Nasar men treated the women who worked for them.

questions.stem: What role does Clotilde Armenta play?
options: She is Angela's friend, who taught her how to fake her virginity on the night
She is Santiago's cook, who knows of the plan but says nothing
She owns the milk shop where the twins wait, and tries to get them stopped
She owns the milk shop where the twins wait, and urges them to act
questions.explanation: The twins wait in Clotilde's shop with their knives. She urges the mayor to act and finally shouts to Santiago to run, one of the few who really tries.

questions.stem: What real event inspired the novella?
options: A 1951 duel in Sucre between two families over some disputed farmland
A 1951 killing in Aracataca, the author's birthplace, over a land feud
A 1951 killing in Sucre, Colombia, after a bride was returned to her family
A 1951 killing in Sucre, Colombia, after a dispute over an unpaid family debt
questions.explanation: In 1951 in Sucre, a bride was returned to her family on her wedding night, and her brother killed the man she named. García Márquez knew the people involved and waited years to write about it.

questions.stem: What does the 'code of honour' in the novella mainly demand?
options: That men avenge any shame to the family, especially concerning women's virginity
That a bride's family pay a generous dowry before any wedding can go ahead
That families settle their disputes through the courts rather than private revenge
That a man accused of dishonour defend himself in a public duel
questions.explanation: A family's honour rests on its daughters' virginity, and the brothers are expected to restore it with violence. Many townspeople accept this, which is why so few intervene.

questions.stem: How does the novella present the Catholic Church?
options: As powerful in the town's life but useless in preventing the murder
As a source of comfort that helps the town come to terms with the death
As a strong moral voice that the townspeople choose to ignore that day
As corrupt, with a priest who arranges Angela's marriage for money
questions.explanation: The bishop never steps off his boat, and Father Amador, who heard of the plan, did not act. He later performs a brutal autopsy. Faith is everywhere in the town, but it saves no one.

questions.stem: Why is the title word 'Chronicle' significant?
options: Angela calls her letters to Bayardo a chronicle of her years of waiting
García Márquez was a journalist, and the book reads like a reconstructed report
The novella is a diary that Santiago kept in the last days before he was killed
The town's newspaper is called the Chronicle, and the narrator works for it
questions.explanation: A chronicle records events, and the narrator gathers testimony like a reporter. Yet the facts never add up to a clear truth, which is part of the novella's point.

questions.stem: Which question lies at the heart of the novella?
options: How a murder that everyone knew about could still happen
Who really killed Santiago Nasar, since no one saw it
Whether Bayardo will return to marry Angela again
Why the bishop refused to bless the town that day
questions.explanation: The killers and the outcome are known from the start. What the narrator investigates is why a whole town, warned many times, let it happen.

questions.stem: How does the novella explore collective responsibility?
options: The twins act alone and in secret, so the town learns of their plan only afterwards
The mayor is blamed as the one official who could have stopped it
Many people warn Santiago, but he is too proud to listen to them
Many people know of the plan but assume someone else will act or that it is a bluff
questions.explanation: Some think it is drunken talk, some are busy with the bishop, some think Santiago already knows, and a few want him dead. The guilt is spread across the community, not held by the twins alone.

questions.stem: What does the novella suggest about fate?
options: Chance and choices combine so the death seems fated, yet people could have stopped it
Santiago's death is fated by omens, so no one in the town can be blamed
Fate is irrelevant, as the twins' careful planning explains every event
Coincidence alone kills Santiago, since the whole town does its very best to save him
questions.explanation: Dreams, omens and coincidences make the death feel destined. But each failure to warn him was a human choice, so the novella resists letting anyone hide behind fate.

questions.stem: How does the novella present the position of women in the town?
options: Women are judged by their virginity, but men in the town are judged just as harshly for their affairs
Women are judged by their virginity and raised to marry and suffer, while men face little judgement
Women are treated as men's equals at home, but must obey the Church's rules
Women are free to choose their husbands, though their families advise them
questions.explanation: Angela is beaten and shamed, while no one questions Bayardo's or Santiago's conduct. The Vicario daughters were 'raised to suffer', brought up only to marry, which exposes the double standard.

questions.stem: What is the effect of revealing the ending in the first sentence?
options: Suspense shifts from whether Santiago dies to how and why no one stopped it
Suspense shifts to who the killers are, as they are revealed only at the end
Suspense disappears, so the reader's interest moves to Angela's love story
Readers are led to doubt the narrator until the death is finally confirmed
questions.explanation: Knowing the outcome, readers watch each missed chance with growing dread. The title itself 'foretells' the death too.

questions.stem: How does the narrator build his account of the murder?
options: By interviewing the twins alone, whose story he accepts without question
By collecting the often conflicting memories of many witnesses and records
By relying on his own clear memory of everything he saw that morning
By following the investigating judge's report, which settles each doubt about the day
questions.explanation: Witnesses disagree even about the weather that morning. The narrator's patchwork of testimony shows how unreliable memory is and how hard it is to reach the truth.

questions.stem: How do dreams and omens function in the novella?
options: Santiago's dream of trees is misread by his mother, adding to the sense of doom
Santiago dreams of the twins' knives, so he hides at home until the bishop arrives
Plácida reads her son's dream as a warning, but he ignores her advice
Dreams reveal the twins' plan to Santiago, who dismisses them as nonsense
questions.explanation: Plácida Linero, known for reading dreams, misses the warning in her son's dream. Omens like this give the story a mood of fate and a touch of magic realism.

questions.stem: Which best describes the novella's genre?
options: A conventional detective novel in which the killer is unmasked in the final chapter
A straightforward work of journalism that reports the real 1951 events faithfully
A work of magic realism in which supernatural events drive the plot forward
A mix of journalism and fiction, using the form of a detective story without its mystery
questions.explanation: It looks like crime reportage but tells us the killers at once. García Márquez borrows the detective form to investigate a community rather than solve a crime.

questions.stem: The narrator says 'There had never been a death more foretold.' What does this line emphasise?
options: That the twins had planned the murder in secret for many months
That the whole town believed Santiago deserved the death that came to him
That almost everyone knew of the killing beforehand, yet it still happened
That Santiago had dreamed of his death every night for many years
questions.explanation: The line echoes the title. It points to the novella's central puzzle: a death announced to so many people that it should have been impossible.

questions.stem: What are Santiago's last words, spoken as he reaches the back of his house?
options: 'Tell Flora that I am innocent'
'I did not do it, I swear to God'
'They've killed me, Wene child'
'Mother, why did you lock the door?'
questions.explanation: His last words are plain and almost calm. He walks into his kitchen and falls, still behaving with his usual composure, which makes the scene more shocking.

questions.stem: Clotilde Armenta begs the twins, 'Leave him for later, if only out of respect for his grace the bishop.' What does this show?
options: The twins are deeply religious and will obey any request about the bishop
The bishop has ordered that no one in the town be harmed during his visit
Even those who object to the killing frame it as something to delay, not stop
Clotilde wants Santiago dead and hopes the twins will kill him after the visit
questions.explanation: Clotilde does want the murder prevented, but her plea appeals to the bishop's visit rather than to the wrongness of killing. It shows how deeply the code of honour shapes even objections to it.

questions.stem: Witnesses who heard the twins at the market said, 'We thought it was drunkards' baloney.' What does this reveal?
options: How the twins disguised their threat as a joke so no one would interfere
How easily people dismissed the threat rather than taking responsibility
How the witnesses believed Santiago deserved whatever the twins did
How the witnesses feared the twins too much to report what they had heard
questions.explanation: Treating the threat as drunken talk let people avoid acting. It is one of many excuses the narrator collects to show how the town failed Santiago.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'In Chronicle of a Death Foretold, the whole town is guilty of murder.' Discuss.
options: Chronicle of a Death Foretold is a short novella that was first published in 1981
García Márquez suggests that the townspeople's silence makes them share the twins' guilt
In Chronicle of a Death Foretold, Santiago Nasar is killed by the Vicario twins one morning
This essay will discuss the guilt of the town in the novella by Gabriel García Márquez
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Santiago's mother locks the front door.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Explain the irony that the act meant to protect him is what traps him
State that the locked door is an important symbol in the novella
Quote the exact sentence that describes the door being barred
Describe what happens next in the order that the events occur
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the detail suggests. Linking the locked door to irony and fate turns a plot event into evidence for an argument.
